extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematics students (researchers, graduate students, and others doing mathematical work)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on keeping permanent sketches/notes of mathematical arguments — how to record, store, format, and (optionally) publish informal or incomplete work so it can be recovered and reused later. Aimed at researchers and students doing mathematical research or expository work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write down sketches of any interesting argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down (preferably on a computer) a sketch of any interesting argument you come across — not necessarily at a publication level of quality, but detailed enough that you can later reconstruct the argument from the sketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tao emphasizes making the argument permanently available to yourself; the sketch should be 'detailed enough that I could then safely forget about the details, and readily recover the argument from the sketch whenever the need arises.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Record non-publishable or rough ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an idea does not rise to the level of originality and depth required for a publishable paper, consider writing it up and keeping it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such sketches can later be helpful in papers, lecture notes, teaching, or proposals; they need not be polished or final to be useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write informal sketches for abandoned or incomplete arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have an incomplete (or otherwise unsatisfactory) argument that you are planning to abandon, still write an informal sketch giving barely enough details to allow you to readily reconstruct the whole thing later on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Store these sketches somewhere on your computer; they may be useful in the future even if the idea is abandoned now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use writing as practice to develop mathematical and expository skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing notes gives you practice in mathematical writing, both technically (e.g. learning to use TeX) and at an expository or pedagogical level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat note-writing as training: it helps you learn presentation, exposition, and the technical toolchain used in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use writing to test whether you truly understand an argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing up an argument tests whether you have really understood it on more than just a superficial level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process of recording an argument reveals gaps in understanding and forces clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your sketches/notes available (e.g., on your website)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you have written up a sketch, you might consider making it available (e.g., on your web site), even if it does not rise to the level required for a publishable paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public availability increases the chance the material will be useful to others and yourself later; blogs or personal webpages are suggested venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Back up your notes and files
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep backups of your computer files (e.g., by using a cloud-based file storage system such as Dropbox).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Backing up prevents accidental loss of the sketches you rely on to reconstruct arguments later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer content-oriented, text-based formats (TeX) for collaboration and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: For collaboration or submitting to journals/publishers, use a content-oriented, text-based format such as TeX and its relatives rather than WYSIWYG tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: journals and arXiv are optimised for TeX; many journals supply .sty files to ease conversion; plain text formats are easier for collaborators and for copyediting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain text/TeX to ease collaboration and version control
rubrics_metrics.description: It is easier to collaborate with plain text formats (such as .tex files) than with richer formats for technical reasons (e.g., you can work on separate sections separately and use version control software to track changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt version control and sectioned workflows to collaborate effectively; richer binary/WYSIWYG formats make these workflows harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve WYSIWYG editors for single-author, self-published work
rubrics_metrics.description: A custom WYSIWYG editor is appropriate for single-author, self-published articles, but is less suitable when collaborating or aiming for publication in journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WYSIWYG can be convenient for solitary work, but conversion/import/export issues and lack of compatibility with collaborators/journal workflows make TeX preferable in collaborative/publishing contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't customise presentation prematurely
rubrics_metrics.description: Because peer review means you cannot ensure in advance which journal will publish your article, there is little point in using WYSIWYG tools to customise presentation before submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on content in a standard format (TeX); journals' .sty files usually make conversion to house style straightforward later.
